sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic focus-group study of language loss; no phonology, no word list; p.222 repeats that 'the only source of Pijao words was' the Loukotka list and Ramirez Sendoya 1952.

sources.citation: Zwisler, Joshua James. 2018. The Pijao of Natagaima: Post-Linguicide Indigenous Identity and Language. Cadernos de Etnolinguistica 6(1): 51-80.
sources.note: No stress rule for Pijao. p.55: the only Pijao sources are Simon's word list, Ramirez Sendoya 1952 and 'the Loukokta word list (30 words long)'; 'there is also no record either of the morphosyntax of the Pijao language'. p.70: the community-remembered word list from Natagaima (pp. 70-72) is written in an orthography 'based on, but not identical, to the system used by Durbin and Seijas (1973) with diacritics representing stress'; acute accents appear on individual items in final (alaman, tenu, cibilo, curuki), penult (kahirre, golupa, tolema, caguala) and initial (cecira, oreme, tungama, ciu)…

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2015. Change Request Number 2015-042: merge [coy] Coyaima and [nts] Natagaimas into [pij] Pijao (adopted 2016-01-15). SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing on phonology. p.2: 'Any mention of Natagaimas [nts] is missing from all the major sources on South American languages. Hammarstrom (2015) believes that both Coyaima [coy] and Natagaimas [nts] are simply place names and should be merged into Pijao, citing Durbin and Seijas 1973.' Establishes that Natagaimas is not a language distinct from Pijao.
